title: Claude Code Setting Leaks Passwords in 1,100+ Repos
metaDescription: Over 1,100 public GitHub repos expose secrets due to Claude Code's 'Don't Ask Again' setting. Learn how it happens and how to secure your team's workflow.
excerpt: A convenience feature in Anthropic's Claude Code has left API keys and credentials exposed across more than 1,100 public GitHub repositories. Here is what SecOps teams need to know.
content:
Developer convenience and ironclad security have always existed in an uneasy tension, but the rapid proliferation of autonomous command-line AI agents is pushing that friction to a breaking point. A stark reminder emerged this week following research from security firm Apiiro, reported by The Hacker News: over 1,100 public GitHub repositories currently harbor sensitive credentials, tokens, and private API keys leaked directly through an innocuous-looking settings file generated by Anthropic’s Claude Code assistant.

The culprit is not a zero-day exploit or an intricate remote code execution vulnerability. Instead, it is a textbook failure of credential hygiene at the interaction boundary: a simple "Yes, and don't ask again" permission prompt that records raw terminal commands verbatim into a project configuration file.

How "Don't Ask Again" Became an Open Invitation

Claude Code, designed to operate natively within developer terminals, frequently executes shell commands to inspect files, execute builds, run tests, or configure environments. To preserve safety and prevent unintended system modifications, the tool prompts engineers before executing sensitive or potentially destructive commands.

However, continuous confirmation dialogs quickly induce prompt fatigue. To streamline the developer experience, Claude Code offers an option to approve a command permanently: "Yes, and don't ask again."

When an engineer selects this option, the tool persists the approved command string inside a local project configuration file so that future automated runs can proceed without manual intervention. The critical oversight lies in how those inputs are stored. If an engineer executes a command containing an inline secret—such as an environment export, a curl request bearing an authorization bearer token, or a database connection string with embedded passwords—Claude Code saves the command word-for-word, secrets included.

When teams unknowingly commit their project roots to version control without comprehensive .gitignore rules covering Claude’s metadata files, those configuration caches travel straight to remote code hosts. Apiiro discovered at least 1,122 public repositories on GitHub currently exposing plaintext secrets through this exact mechanism.

The Hidden Risks of Agentic CLI Tooling

This incident underscores an emerging class of operational risk unique to generative AI developer tooling:

  • Unsanitized Intent Persistence: When agentic tools remember user approvals, storing raw string inputs rather than parameterized command templates or sanitized patterns guarantees that ephemeral credentials become persistent artifacts.
  • Artifact Invisibility: Developers expect source code to be tracked in Git, but local AI state files, prompt histories, and permission logs frequently blend into project directories without clear visual markers or default ignore rules.
  • Bypassing Environment Variables: Under deadline pressure, developers frequently pass quick API keys via CLI flags, assuming terminal history is their only risk vector. They remain unaware that their AI assistant is silently archiving every parameter to disk.

For security teams and compliance officers, this presents an urgent discovery challenge. Third-party API keys, production database credentials, and cloud tokens pushed to public repositories are indexed by automated malicious scanners within minutes, drastically reducing mean-time-to-compromise.

Actionable Defenses for SecOps and Engineering Leads

Remediating this exposure requires immediate operational hygiene alongside policy adjustments for agent-assisted development environments:

  1. Audit Existing Repositories: Search organizational codebases immediately for committed Claude Code configuration files and verify whether any historical commits contain cached, raw command strings.
  2. Rotate Exposed Credentials Immediately: Treat any key present in a committed configuration file as fully compromised. Revoke and reissue credentials rather than merely purging the file from the latest Git commit.
  3. Update Global Ignore Rules: Mandate organization-wide .gitignore templates that automatically exclude AI metadata files, session logs, and local agent permission stores across all developer workstations.
  4. Strictly Decouple Secrets from CLI Invocations: Re-enforce zero-trust credential habits. Engineers should supply credentials exclusively through system environment variables, local secret managers, or specialized credential helpers—never via inline command arguments.
  5. Strengthen Push Protection: Deploy automated secret scanners at the pre-commit hook level and within CI/CD pipelines to catch non-standard configuration formats before commits ever leave developer endpoints.

Navigating the AI Tooling Era

As agentic AI tools gain deeper autonomy across the software development lifecycle, the boundary between developer intent and persistent configuration is blurring. Claude Code's configuration leak demonstrates that securing AI workflows is no longer just about guarding model weights or validating generated code. IT leaders must now aggressively inspect the secondary digital footprint left behind by the agents assisting their teams.
